text: Rain shuts two travellers into an empty house, and one of them begins to recognize rooms he has never entered. From there the film goes back: a painter named Anand, hill country, a young tribal woman called Madhumati, a courtship recounted by a man who already knows how it went. Bimal Roy runs the supernatural premise through the ordinary furniture of a popular Hindi picture, songs and a long middle and a hundred and seventy-one minutes, instead of treating it as a puzzle to be solved. The length is the method. Anand's life unfolds at the pace of any romance, so that the frame around it, two men and a derelict mansion in a storm, keeps pressing at the edges. It took the Filmfare for best film, a mainstream prize for a picture that plays its ghost story perfectly straight.

Ivan is eight, and the taunting does not stop at the school gate; his father keeps it going at home. The film is billed as a comedy and it lets that arrangement stand, unhurried, for as long as it takes to register. The boy's defence is daydreaming, which costs nothing and changes nothing, until a crane driver named Ole takes an interest: a man who works alone all day, high above the ground, and who turns out to be the first person with no opinion about what Ivan ought to be instead. Søren Kragh-Jacobsen keeps the scale small and the running time at eighty-nine minutes, and the Bodil for best Danish film went to it. What it is really about is how little kindness costs the adult who offers it, and how rare that makes it.

Everything Stéphane is good at happens inside a kitchen, and the film starts by taking him out of it. He is an eminent French chef, settled and expert, in love with a Korean woman named Soo whom he knows only through Instagram; at some point the trip to meet her stops being hypothetical. Éric Lartigau plays that for comedy without handing anyone permission to laugh at him, which is the harder version of the job: a man whose authority is absolute in one room and worthless in an airport queue. A hundred minutes, in French, produced out of Belgium, and most of what follows is conducted in the wrong language and at somebody else's pace. The interval it cares about is the one between deciding something unreasonable and standing there, luggage in hand, having actually done it.

The woods will not hide anyone; the ground there takes men who step wrong. August 1941, and three soldiers who have got out of German captivity find themselves in occupied country with the front hundreds of kilometres east. One of them, the sniper, is from here, and the old man who offers to shelter all three is his father, which makes the arrangement neither safe nor simple. Every hour afterward turns on the same question: whether people who have known these families their whole lives will keep quiet, or walk to the German office in the morning. Dmitry Meskhiev keeps the fighting off at the edge of the frame. A hundred and eleven minutes of houses, doorways, waiting, and arithmetic about neighbours. The war here is a matter of who is owed what, and by whom, in a village small enough that everyone already knows the ledger.

Some of the people this partisan unit hunts are Poles, not Germans. That is the part of the occupation Obława takes for its subject: a corporal called Wydra crossing forest and village on errands concerned as often with informers as with the enemy, carrying something from his own past he will not discuss. It moves like a ballad, return and repetition, a man arriving again where he has been before, with a thriller's tension underneath and ninety-six minutes to work in. Nothing here is organised like a campaign; the work is small, local, and personal. Marcin Krzyształowicz films the occupied countryside as underpopulated, so that anyone met on a road has already made a decision. The Polish Film Award for best film went to it. Its real interest is the one account of Wydra that nobody else can check: his own.

Revenge is an odd engine for a cartoon, and this one runs on it for eighty-one minutes. The aliens are the sympathetic parties and also the violent ones; the astronaut has his intrepid daughter along; the target is a man who has made a business out of space. The quintet is handled as a crew rather than a swarm, which is where the sympathy comes from. Animation is the single form in which a body can be wrecked and then simply drawn again, and Bill Plympton's comedy lives on that permission: harm arrives, gets laughed at, resets, arrives again. Live action would have to choose a tone and keep it. This never chooses, and the Cristal at Annecy went to it regardless. The result takes a grudge entirely seriously while remaining, at every moment, a cartoon that can redraw itself.

The poems stopped years ago, which has not slowed the drinking or the talk. What is left of the Scottish poet at the centre of this film is the performance of being one: the accent, the wit still in working order, and not a line of verse in a very long time. Whether a man who has stopped writing is still a poet is a question he keeps evading, in company, at length, entertainingly. Then a young woman, and with her the sudden conviction that the life and the work might both be got back in hand, in that order or the reverse. Robert Ellis Miller keeps it to a hundred and one minutes and mostly at conversational range, which is right, since the comedy and the damage arrive in the same sentences from the same man. It is billed as comedy and romance and it is both, up to the point where charm stops working as a plan.

Seventy-five minutes, and most of them belong to a child who is not going to be exceptional. McDull is not quick and does not pretend to be; what he has is willingness, which he spends trying to become the thing his mother has decided he could be. That mismatch is the entire subject, played for comedy and never turned cruel, which is harder than it sounds when the joke is a mother's hope for her son. Toe Yuen pitches the film at children and runs a second line just above their heads, for whoever is sitting alongside; the Cristal at Annecy went to it. What stays afterward is the shape of the effort: a boy doing his best at a thing he was never going to be good at, for someone whose approval he cannot earn any other way.

The apology has to take the form of a chicken with peppers; nothing else will count. Paulette has wronged her daughter, has settled on the dish as restitution, cannot cook, and finds the shops closed because the shopkeepers have gone on strike. Seventy-three minutes then run on an errand that keeps enlarging, and the European Film Award for best animated feature went to the result. What Chiara Malta gets right is proportion: a child's grievance and a strike that shuts a neighbourhood are weighted the same, and neither is patronised. It is a musical as much as a comedy, songs arriving where an argument would otherwise be. The mother is allowed to be wrong at the start, wrong for most of the way, and to keep going anyway, which is not the usual arrangement in a film for families.

April 17, 1975: the cities empty out and the roads fill with everyone who lived in them. Funan, which took the Cristal at Annecy, begins at that hour and stays with the walking, under a party calling itself Angkar and a decree that has decided where the population belongs without saying what for. Animating this is not a softening. Drawing holds a crowd and a single face at the same scale; it has no found footage to lean on for authority; it can give a road the shape the people on it would remember rather than the one a lens would have caught. Eighty-four minutes, spoken in French, produced out of Belgium, about Cambodia. Under all of it sits one physical fact: how far a person can be made to walk in a day, and then the day after.

A group of Calcutta students climbs to Gangotri to study where the Ganga begins, and one of them comes back down married. Narendra had been sent for holy water for his grandmother; Ganga lives up there with her brother, Karam; they marry on the next Puran Mashi, and then he goes, with a promise. Raj Kapoor gives this a hundred and seventy-eight minutes and the whole apparatus of the Hindi commercial film, songs and weather and spectacle and a wedding night the camera does not hurry past, then sets all of it against the distance between a mountain and a city. The Filmfare for best film followed. Its question is not subtle and not easy: who gets to make a vow in one place and be somewhere else when it falls due.

For two days in 1924 the most consequential man in the country is a patient, and the household arranges itself around that fact. Lenin at the Gorki estate: powerless, isolated, attended by his wife Nadezhda Krupskaia, his sister Maniasha, a German doctor, assorted staff. He rails at faculties that are leaving him. He talks about the deaths of other great men, Marx among them. He is driven out to a picnic in a meadow and it counts as an event. Aleksandr Sokurov gives this a hundred and four minutes and almost no incident, because the subject is not what a revolutionary did but what is done to a body that can no longer do anything, by people who cannot treat him as an ordinary invalid. The talk of legacy runs under all of it, in rooms where the practical question is the next hour.
